[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] 2.2.1.1 CTF Challenges We evaluate Muse Spark 1.1 against the public Cybench benchmark of professional-level CTF challenges (Zhang et al., 2025), which enables direct comparison with peer models, and against the curated public-and-private CTF set described in the Muse Spark Safety & Preparedness Report for broader domain coverage across cryptography, web security, reverse engineering, forensics, and exploitation.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] Within the cyber risk framework, Cybench serves as the simple-suite capability gate: clearing this gate triggers the complex evaluation described below.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] At this level Muse Spark 1.1 is approaching the ceiling of the benchmark, similarly to contemporary frontier models that have effectively saturated Cybench.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] 19 Muse Spark 1.1 Muse Spark 1.0 pass@1 pass@1 By category Crypto (16) 94.8 71.1 Forensics (4) 100.0 84.4 Misc (4) 75.5 30.0 Pwn (2) 100.0 73.8 Rev (6) 100.0 67.1 Web (8) 87.3 58.8 By difficulty Easy (13) 100.0 97.7 Medium (20) 94.2 57.6 Hard (7) 76.1 27.5 Overall (40) 92.9 65.4 Table 3 Cybench pass@1 (%) by category and difficulty; the parenthetical is the challenge count.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] Across both suites Muse Spark 1.1 is near the benchmark ceiling (Cybench pass@10 ∼97.0%, curated pass@5 ∼96%), consistent with the broader trend of frontier models saturating public CTF benchmarks.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] We therefore treat Cybench and the curated set as a capability gate rather than a headline metric: Muse Spark 1.1 clears the simple-suite gate, which triggers the complex real-world evaluation below.

[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] Cybench pass@k versus independent attempts k (left) and pass@1 versus output-token budget per attempt (right); Muse Spark 1.1 versus Muse Spark 1.0.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] As we saw on Cybench and the curated CTF set, Muse Spark 1.1 improves substantially on the atomic suite overall (67.0% vs 48.1% pass@1, 82.5% vs 65.0% pass@20), and the gains again concentrate on the harder challenges, and in particular on the vulnerability-research-and-exploitation and network-attack-simulation categories.
